It's what every other line of JavaScript has taught us.

reads like an assignment with a function call around it. Folklore adds "setState is async", which suggests that waiting would help. And there is a true part: React does process the update later, after your handler finishes. What the belief misses is that the variable in your handler never changes at all, no matter how long you wait.
Each render gets its own copy of state
React keeps state outside your component. When it renders
hands back the current value, and

stores it in a constant that belongs to that one call of your function. Event handlers created during that render close over that constant. The docs call this a snapshot: props, handlers and local variables are all computed from the state at the time of the render, and a state variable's value never changes within a render.
A setter queues an update for the next render
. It adds "replace with 120" to a queue for that piece of state and requests a render. React waits until all the code in the event handler has run, then processes the queue and renders once. This is

React runs your updater functions during the next render, not when you call the setter, and Strict Mode runs each one twice in development. An updater should only compute and return the next value: no requests, no mutations and no setting other state from inside it.

items.text: Inside one render, a state variable is a constant snapshot; setters never change it.
A setter queues an update and requests a render; React processes the queue after the handler finishes.
Need the new value right away? Compute it in a local variable and use that; waiting never refreshes the snapshot.
